title: Open questions, kindly
hookLine: Sikhs discuss the Ragmala, the calendar, diet and the Dasam Granth

lines: TWO MEN, ONE TABLE, ONE ARGUMENT.
cards: The program is over and the langar hall is emptying. At the end of one long row, two older men are still at it over steel cups of tea.

One says the gurpurab dates should follow the old moon calendar, the way his grandfather kept them. The other says a fixed solar calendar makes more sense for Sikhs scattered across the world. Neither raises his voice.

A teenager comes by with the kettle and fills both cups without being asked. The argument goes on, and so does the tea. Today opens a week of questions Sikhs are still talking about, and the way they hold them.

teach.b: Sikhs name several questions out loud that the panth hasn't closed. Which calendar should set the dates of the gurpurabs. Whether an initiated Sikh may eat meat.
Who wrote which parts of the Dasam Granth. And the Ragmala, a list of ragas at the very end of the Guru Granth Sahib, which some Sikhs recite at the close of a full reading and others leave out.
On that last one, the Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, doesn't pretend the matter is settled.

teach.h: THE CODE ADMITS THE RAGMALA DEBATE.
teach.b: Its readers point to a line that admits Sikhs hold differing opinions on reading the Ragmala, and then asks only that no copy of the Granth be written or printed without it. The question stays open. The book stays whole.
That's a way of holding a disagreement: decide what you must, leave room where you can, and protect the thing everyone shares.
On Ang 661, Guru Nanak says, here in paraphrase, that as long as we are in this world, we should listen to something and say something.
Listening comes first in that line, and talk is part of a life of faith, not a failure of it.
Sikhs have a word for this kind of thinking-through: vichar, reflection, turning a thing over carefully.

Over the next days this path takes the questions one at a time: meat, the Dasam Granth, women among the five who serve amrit. It won't settle them. It will try to say each side the way its own people would.

how: Sikhs discuss open questions such as the Ragmala, the calendar for gurpurabs, diet and the Dasam Granth in gurdwaras, homes and conferences, while the Rehat Maryada notes a difference of opinion on reading the Ragmala and asks that every copy of the Granth include it.

games.q: Sikhs differ on whether to recite the Ragmala. you're writing the code of conduct. what do you do?
o: pick a side and ban the other.

games.why: readers of the Rehat Maryada point to exactly this: it notes the difference of opinion and asks that no copy be made without the Ragmala.

practice: Bring to mind one small question people you love disagree about, and give the side you don't hold its best sentence, the one its kindest defender would say.
Breathe in on that sentence and out on your own, and let both sit at the same table a while, like the two cups of tea; if you pray, rest on Waheguru while they sit there.

wordCard.voice: Open questions. The things Sikhs are still talking through, like the Ragmala and the calendar, held inside a shared faith rather than splitting it. Today's word.
